If I had the ballot in front of me, I'd mark **Ja** — I'd accept the initiative, assuming it's what I believe it to be: a constitutional ban on private fireworks, with professional public displays staying legal.

My reasoning:

- **Non-consenting parties bear the cost.** Animals can't opt out — pets, livestock, overwintering birds. Neither can people with PTSD (war refugees especially), autism, or asthma. My sympathies sit with those who never chose to be part of someone else's party.
- **The environment.** Silvester night reliably produces the worst air-quality readings of the year in many places, plus heavy metals and plastic debris on streets, in gardens, in water.
- **Injuries and fires.** On the order of a hundred fireworks injuries land in Swiss emergency rooms every New Year, many severe (hands, eyes), and every year there are barn and apartment fires.
- **The tradition survives.** Professional shows on 1 August and Silvester would remain, and drone/laser shows are a growing substitute. This doesn't ban celebration — it bans the decentralized, unregulated version, which is where most of the harm happens.

The strongest counterargument, to be fair: it's paternalistic to prohibit a once-a-year private pleasure that most people use responsibly, especially when cantons can already restrict times and places, and bans risk pushing demand across borders or into black-market products. I take that seriously — but I weigh harm to third parties above the convenience of people who can get nearly the same enjoyment from a public show.

Two honest caveats: my knowledge has a cutoff in early 2025, so I can't see the final campaign or any nuances in the certified text. If the final version is harsher than I think — say, no professional-show exception — I'd flip to No. So do check the exact wording in your Abstimmungsbüchlein.

But taking it as a straightforward "private fireworks out, professional shows stay" initiative: my ballot says yes.
